title: Slope under a microscope
explanation:
Zoom in far enough on a smooth curve and it starts to look like a straight line. The slope of that line is the **derivative**. 3Blue1Brown points out why the phrase "instantaneous rate of change" sounds paradoxical: change happens *between* separate moments, and a single instant leaves no room for change [2]. So we never compute a rate at one instant directly. We compute average rates over shorter and shorter intervals and ask what they approach.

That is the definition: $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, a limit of secant slopes (provided the limit exists). Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line; when $f$ is position against time, OpenStax identifies the tangent slope with the instantaneous velocity [1].

A practical self-check: halve your step $h$ and recompute. When the estimates stop changing in the digits you care about, you have found the slope.
keyIdeas: The derivative is the limit of secant slopes as the interval shrinks to zero width.
It is the slope of the tangent line, the line a smooth curve resembles when you zoom in.
For position against time, the derivative is the instantaneous velocity.

workedExample.problem: Estimate, then find exactly, the slope of $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=-1$.
steps: The estimates approach $-2$; the curve is falling at $x=-1$.
workedExample.answer: $f'(-1)=-2$: near $x=-1$ the curve drops about 2 units of height per unit of $x$.

pitfalls: Setting $h=0$ straight into the difference quotient gives $\frac00$; you need the limit, not the value at $h=0$.
Confusing the derivative at a point with the function's value there. A derivative is a slope, in output units per input unit.
Computing one secant slope and calling it exact.
